title: Legal Translation
src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2015). Arabic–English–Arabic Translation: Issues and Strategies, ch. 3 “Legal translation”, pp. 94–164. Routledge.

p: Legalese is known for passive verbs, impersonality, nominalizations, long idea-packed sentences, difficult words, double negatives and poor layout, and readers outside the profession often cannot follow it. Yet legal language reaches everyone: a toaster warranty, the terms on a plane ticket or any official form brings words like ‘liability’ and ‘compliance’ into daily life.

Three things set it apart. It has to speak to experts and lay readers at once. In law, language is both the tool and the thing studied, so words are the law’s ‘chemical elements’. And it changes very slowly: a statute may read like one written two hundred years ago, sometimes because it must in order to be valid. That need to comply explains much of its formulaic style.
list: Prescriptive (regulatory) texts impose obligations with sanctions: constitutions, treaties, laws, contracts.

Descriptive texts are still legal instruments but not normative: declarative (witness statements, affidavits), directive (a lawyer’s brief), exhortatory (petitions), expressive (closing arguments), commissive (marriage vows, wills).
Metalegal texts talk about the law (textbooks, articles on jurisprudence) and are not legal instruments themselves.
By producer: legislative, judicial, scholarly and private texts (wills, agreements).
sections.note: Real documents mix categories: a witness statement is both expressive and exhortatory. So it is better to speak of ‘languages of the law’ than one legal register. The audience also varies, from one person to a state, and spoken legal language is less formal and less binding (verba volant).

p: Unlike chemistry, which is the same everywhere, law is tied to a system and a culture, so the legal translator has to know how the law works in both communities. You need not be a lawyer, but you must understand the legal effect a sentence is meant to have and how to get that effect in the other language. The aim is to say what the legislator meant ‘and in the way they customarily say it’.

The two main families are Common Law (judge-made, case law; England, the USA, Canada, Ireland, Australia) and Civil Law (codified statutes; continental Europe, rooted in Roman law). Systems mix: Louisiana and Quebec have Civil Law roots; Algeria, Morocco, Syria and Tunisia have French-style Civil Law alongside Islamic law; Oman’s system draws on English Common Law. Islamic law (شَرِيعة), sourced in the Qur’an and Sunnah and extended by إِجْماع (consensus) and قِياس (analogy), applies in Arab states beside a secular code, or alone, as in Saudi Arabia.

Arabic legal drafting can be literary and elevated (the preambles of several Arab constitutions), while English drafting aims to be concise and precise. Common Law judgments are long, because they cite precedent; Civil Law statutes state principles broadly, while Common Law statutes define everything.
list: The faithfulness argument (the letter of the law, precision, penalties for deviation) is weaker than it looks: translation always interprets, and some ambiguity is deliberate and must be kept.
Contracts often contain business, finance or engineering terms: the legal translator must know the subject matter too.
System-bound terms cluster around the profession (solicitor, القاضي), the courts (High Court, مَحْكَمة شَرْعِيّة) and areas of law (equity, اجْتِهاد).
ex: Law No 73 of 1956 · In the name of the Nation · Having reviewed … · Has issued the following law:
قانون رقم 73 لسنة 1956 · باسم الأمة · بعد الاطلاع على … · أصدر القانون الآتي:
We, Qaboos Bin Said, Sultan of Oman, after perusal of … Have Decreed as Follows
نحن قابوس بن سعيد، سلطان عمان … بعد الاطلاع على … رسمنا بما هو آت
BE IT ENACTED by the Queen’s most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of …
(UK enacting formula; Arabic has no fixed equivalent and follows its own formulas)

p: The same system can name things differently. Lawyer, attorney, solicitor, barrister, advocate and counsel can all be مُحامٍ in Arabic, but they are not synonyms. In the UK an ‘attorney’ acts for someone else (وَكِيل; power of attorney, سَنَد التَّوْكِيل); the solicitor/barrister split does not exist in the USA; Scotland says advocate. In the Maghreb, a عَدْل (pl. عُدُول) is a judge’s assistant who does a notary’s work (كاتِب عَدْل).

Identical names do not mean identical courts: New Zealand’s High Court corresponds to the US or UK Supreme Court, and ‘District Court’ means different things in Ireland, the USA and Scotland. Think in terms of equivalence, not word-for-word. Dictionary paraphrases such as ‘local courts with special competence limited to the area over which they have jurisdiction’ are not usable translations.
Arab court names show their Civil Law origins in French calques (Court of Cassation, Court of First Instance), which British and American English use only for continental courts.

sections.h: Legislative bodies: use the official names
p: Each Arab country has its own official English name for its legislature. The same Arabic term does not mean the same English one, nor that the body works the same way.

rows: Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Morocco, Yemen / Lebanon / Tunisia
Council of Representatives; House of Representatives / National Assembly / Chamber of Deputies
Algeria / Egypt / Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Yemen
Shura Council / Advisory Council / Consultative Council
Assembly of Councillors / Chamber of Councillors

p: Operative documents (wills, birth certificates) follow fixed layouts; statutes are rigid too. A UK Act runs: short title, long title, enacting formula, then Parts, Chapters, cross-headings and numbered sections. Australia uses Chapter–Part–Division–Section; in US Acts, ‘Section’ and ‘Title’ correspond to the UK ‘Part’ and ‘Chapter’.

Today’s practice is to make the translation mirror the source layout as closely as possible, especially for forms and certificates, including bold, italics and underlining. In Arabic–English work the trend is to flip everything into mirror image for the new script direction. Put signatures, stamps and photos in square brackets: [STAMP: …], [signature].

Arabic marks emphasis with font changes (it has no capitals) and uses bold heavily; English frowns on mixed fonts and keeps bold for headings and vital information, using capitals and bold to show hierarchy.

p: Ideally one legal concept has one term, but polysemy is everywhere. ‘Law’ alone covers a rule, the body of law, the police (‘The law was on the heels of the fugitive’, كانَتِ الشُّرْطةُ تَتَعَقَّبُ الهارِبَ), a branch of study and a law of nature (النَّوامِيس الطَّبِيعِيّة).

Arabic dictionaries list many words for ‘law’, and several belong only to Islamic law, so they must never be used for secular law. For ‘lawful’, only قانُونِيّ and شَرْعِيّ are secular; حَلال is religious.

rows: Law as a subject of study (capital L: ‘He studied Law’)

list: قَرار covers resolution (Security Council resolution, قَرار مَجْلِسِ الأَمْن), award (arbitral award, قَرار التَّحْكِيم), adjudication, decision, order, indictment and ruling.
لائِحة covers indictment (لائِحة اتِّهام), regulation (Council Regulations), bill (true bill) and rule (administrative rule).
قاعِدة covers rule (substantive rule, قاعِدة مَوْضُوعِيّة; peremptory rule, قاعِدة آمِرة), database, base, norm, jus (jus soli, قاعِدة حَقِّ الأَرْض) and lex (lex specialis, قاعِدة التَّخْصِيص).
مَرْسُوم covers decree (royal decree, مَرْسُوم مَلَكِيّ) and ruling (Ruling on the General Amnesty, مَرْسُوم العَفْوِ العامّ).

Dictionaries offer nine verbs for ‘comply’ (أَطاعَ, طاوَعَ, اسْتَكانَ, امْتَثَلَ, ذَعِنَ, أَذْعَنَ, قَبِلَ, اسْتَجابَ, راعَى), but they are not synonyms: اسْتَكانَ is ‘to surrender’ and never legal. And ‘in compliance with’ is none of them: it is عَمَلاً بِـ.
Archaisms: aforesaid, heretofore, witnesseth.
Latin (Roman occupation, the Church, Norman law): mens rea (نِيّة جُرْمِيّة), sub iudice (أَمامَ القاضي), viva voce (شَفَوِيّاً).
Norman French, the language of the courts until 1362: naturalized forms (crime, جَرِيمة; verdict, قَرار) and unchanged ones (sans frais, دُونَ نَفَقة; tort, جَرِيرة شَخْصِيّة).
Polysemy: ‘seize’ means to impound (حَجَزَ), to arrest (قَبَضَ عَلَى), or for the Security Council ‘to remain seized of the matter’ (يُقَرِّرُ أَنْ يُبْقِيَ المَسْأَلةَ قَيْدَ نَظَرِهِ الفِعْلِيّ).
p: Binomial pairs and doublets are fixed legal idioms. Arabic usually renders the whole pair with one word, though occasionally a pair is kept (خالِص ومُطْلَق ‘free and clear’). In the other direction, decide whether بَيْن is plain ‘between’ or formulaic ‘by and between’; most translators follow the target genre’s expectations.

rows: by and between; between and among

p: Islamic legal terms have no ready English equivalents, and the strategy depends on readership and text type: a marriage contract between Muslims keeps more borrowed terms than a trade contract. Usage also varies by region: religious endowments are وَقْف (pl. أَوْقاف) in the East and حَبْس (pl. حُبُوس) in North Africa.

بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ has competing translations (‘In the Name of God/Allah, the Compassionate, the Merciful’; ‘the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate’; ‘the Most Beneficent, the Most Merciful’). It used to be left out of legal translations; today it is increasingly kept, and it should never be dropped from certificates and forms.

Titles: legal translation is more literal than general translation, so titles and formulas are usually kept, with English equivalents and blessings in square brackets. Translating into Arabic, add the expected titles and formulas so the text is accepted.

rows: طَلاق بائِن irrevocable divorce · حُجّة certificate · مَهْر dowry
القاضي; Islamic judge · عِدّة legally prescribed waiting period before marrying · ثَيِّب deflowered woman · دُخُول consummation of marriage
فَقِيه faqih · رِبا riba · حِجاب hijab · وَقْف waqf

ex: The Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al Saud [May God protect him] chaired the Cabinet session.
رَأَسَ خادِمُ الحَرَمَيْنِ الشَّرِيفَيْنِ المَلِكُ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ عَبْدِ العَزِيزِ آلِ سُعُود – حَفِظَهُ اللهُ – الجَلْسَةَ الَّتي عَقَدَها مَجْلِسُ الوُزَراءِ

sections.h: Shared features: jargon, homonyms, repetition, collocation
p: Both languages have core jargon: courts, professions, ‘pursuant to’, ‘liability’ (مَسْؤُولِيّة), ‘to remand’ (أَعادَ الدَّعْوَى). The twenty most frequent words in a Leeds Arabic legal corpus are all technical: المادة، القانون، المحكمة، المتهم، القضاء، الدعوى، حقوق، قرار، الدستور، الجنائية، القضائية، النيابة، الحكم، الجرائم، التحقيق، الأمن، الشرطة، التعذيب، يجوز، السلطة. Even ‘Graduation Certificate’ varies by country: إِفادة التَّخَرُّج (Libya), وَثِيقة التَّخَرُّج (Saudi Arabia), شَهادة التَّخَرُّج (Tunisia, Oman).

Repetition is the norm, not a fault. Legal texts repeat the same noun phrase (‘the Company’, never ‘the Firm’) and list every contingency (‘war, hostilities, invasion, acts by foreign enemies, rebellion …’), with phrases like ‘including but not limited to’. Do not tidy this away.

Collocations decide meaning. رَفَعَ دَعْوَى ضِدَّ … أَمامَ … is ‘to file a complaint against … in …’ or simply ‘to sue’; أَقامَ دَعْوَى also works. ‘Commit a crime’ is ارْتَكَبَ / اقْتَرَفَ جَرِيمة, but back-translating ‘carry out’ as نَفَّذَ or أَنْجَزَ fails: those go with مَشْرُوع, اخْتِبار, بَرْنامَج. With حُكْم: نَفَّذَ (execute), صادَقَ عَلَى (confirm), صَدَرَ (be issued), أَصْدَرَ (pass), اسْتَصْدَرَ (obtain), أَلْغَى (rescind), طَعَنَ في (appeal against), طالَبَ بِـ (demand), رَفَضَ (reject).

Countries now publish their own official translations, and these set precedents that later translations must follow, even when better wording is possible. Research what is in use. Oman calls its ministry the ‘Ministry of Legal Affairs’ (وزارة الشؤون القانونية) where others say وزارة العدل; وزارة الخارجية is the Foreign Office (UK), State Department (USA) or Ministry of Foreign Affairs (elsewhere).
This also applies to certificates, the freelancer’s ‘bread and butter’: follow established models or a sworn translation may be rejected.

sections.h: Syntax: long sentences, the passive, shall and may
sections.ar: التركيب: الجملة الطويلة والمبني للمجهول وshall/may
p: Legal English has the longest sentences of any genre: one official sentence ran to 516 words. Typical features include the formulaic subjunctive (‘Be it enacted’), inversion, long sub-clauses, adjectives placed after the noun (‘Lords Spiritual’), and chains of ‘and’. The Universal Declaration preamble stacks ‘Whereas …’ clauses before the main clause (‘Now, therefore, The General Assembly proclaims …’); Arabic opens each with لَمّا كانَ / وَلَمّا كانَ and resolves it with فَإِنَّ الجَمْعِيّةَ العامّةَ.

The passive: legal English uses it heavily, Arabic dislikes it, and classical rules forbid naming the agent. Strategies: an Arabic passive, an active, reflexive forms (V, VII, VIII), تَمَّ / يَتِمُّ + verbal noun, or nominalization. Agent phrases (بِواسِطة, مِنْ قِبَل, مِنْ طَرَف) are calques considered substandard but now common in legal texts.

Shall is never a future in legal English; it is an obligation, like ‘must’. May is permission, and ‘may not’ is a prohibition. Performative declarations use a simple present (‘This Regulation is hereby repealed’). Arabic can use عَلَى, يَجِبُ عَلَى, لا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ / أَنْ or يَنْبَغِي, but very often renders ‘shall’ with a plain imperfect.
The declarative ‘do’ (‘We the People … do ordain’) works like ‘hereby’ with performative verbs; it is never translated, and the verb becomes an imperfect.
ex: The work shall be performed by the subcontractor.
يَتِمُّ تَنْفِيذُ العَمَلِ بِواسِطَةِ المُقاوِلِ
The proposed budget shall be reviewed by the Committee.
تَقُومُ اللَّجْنَةُ بِمُراجَعَةِ المِيزانِيَّةِ المُقْتَرَحَةِ
After the director is dismissed, the company will withdraw.
بَعْدَ عَزْلِ المُدِيرِ سَتَنْسَحِبُ الشَّرِكَةُ مِنَ المَشْرُوعِ
Decides that all Member States shall immediately take the necessary measures to prevent …
يُقَرِّرُ أَنْ تَتَّخِذَ جَمِيعُ الدُّوَلِ الأَعْضاءِ فَوْراً التَّدابِيرَ اللّازِمَةَ لِمَنْعِ …
Each State Party shall adopt such measures as may be necessary.
تَتَّخِذُ كُلُّ دَوْلَةٍ طَرَفٍ التَّدابِيرَ اللّازِمَةَ
Each person … shall be entitled to …
يَحِقُّ لِأَيِّ شَخْصٍ …
The contractor shall not purchase products or services without prior approval from the owner.
يَتَعَهَّدُ المُقاوِلُ بِعَدَمِ شِراءِ مُنْتَجاتٍ أَوْ خِدْماتٍ بِدُونِ مُوافَقَةٍ مُسْبَقَةٍ مِنَ المالِكِ
The Distributor does agree that he is responsible for the cost of reassembly.
يُوافِقُ المُوَزِّعُ عَلَى أَنْ يَكُونَ مَسْؤُولاً عَنْ تَكْلِفَةِ إِعادَةِ التَّجْمِيعِ
Whereas recognition of the inherent dignity … is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world,
لَمّا كانَ الاعْتِرافُ بِالكَرامَةِ المُتَأَصِّلَةِ في جَمِيعِ أَعْضاءِ الأُسْرَةِ البَشَرِيَّةِ … هُوَ أَساسَ الحُرِّيَّةِ وَالعَدْلِ وَالسَّلامِ في العالَمِ

p: Arabic–English legal dictionaries are scarce and uneven, so the translator’s main tools are model documents: ministry law databases, and UN material, where Arabic is an official language so parallel texts are easy to find.

p: The chapter ends with annotated sample translations that work well for practice. Arabic into English: a civil marriage contract (following the Hanafi school, with notes on dowry, witnesses and formulas), an Arab Open University graduation certificate, Morocco’s Press Act No 77-00 and an employment contract. English into Arabic: a Zanussi-Electrolux guarantee and a rental agreement, with exercises.
